frase_gancho.texto: Copal and rubber smoke to call the gods.

puente_narrativo.texto: The smoke rises toward the sky, and in the morning sky shines the star that Tula worshipped. Head to the tombstone of the Lord of the Dawn and the story of a king who became a star.

guion_corto.texto: This clay brazier was used to burn copal, the aromatic resin of certain trees, and rubber, which burns with a thick black smoke. It is modeled with applied clay decoration: strips, little balls, and figures of clay stuck to the surface to form the ornaments. Look at the human face that decorates it. Braziers like this one were lit on the altars of temples during state ceremonies, and the smoke rose to the sky as food and message for the gods. It is a simple object, but it turned an entire plaza into a sacred cloud. And behind the scent lay a whole idea of the world: what is burned disappears from here and appears there.

guion_largo.texto:
If you close your eyes at a ceremony in Tula, the first thing you notice is not what you see, but what you smell. Copal, the resin of trees from the hot lands, was burned in these braziers and spread a sweet, resinous scent across the plaza. Smoke was the way the living communicated with the gods: what is burned here rises and arrives there. The word “copal,” by the way, also comes from Nahuatl: copalli.

But the brazier did not burn only copal. Rubber was burned as well, the latex of the tree from which the balls for the ballgame were made. When it burns, rubber produces a thick black smoke, which rose in dark columns. It is thought that this smoke had to do with storm clouds: it was a way of calling the rain. The ballcourt marker of La Ventilla and these braziers of Tula have something in common: the same tree.

Notice how it is decorated. The technique is called applied clay decoration: the potter made little balls, strips, and figures of clay, and stuck them one by one onto the surface, like someone decorating a cake. With them, scrolls, borders, and ornaments are formed. It is a slow technique that demands patience, and it has the advantage of giving relief. To the eye, it looks like a sculpture made of pieces stuck together.

The human face is the part that draws the most attention. We do not know for certain who it is. It could be a god, an ancestor, or a priest. What we do know is that the custom of placing a face on the brazier comes from Teotihuacán: there, the “theater-type” braziers had a mask at the center. In Tula, the idea continues, but the potters gave it their own style.

This brazier brings us back to the Old God of Fire. If you remember the stone figure that carries the vessel on his head, this object is his descendant: the vessel of fire, now without an old man to carry it. Fire, in Mesoamerica, was a god. Lighting it was not a technical act: it was a way of praying.

Now imagine a state ceremony in Tula. Dozens of braziers lit in the plazas, along the stairways, atop the pyramids. A cloud of perfumed smoke rises from the center of the city toward the sky, visible from far away. The power of the city is also experienced as scent and as smoke, not only as stone.

There is an irony. Around the year 1150, the center of Tula was destroyed by a fire. One of the buildings that burned is known today as the Palacio Quemado, a name given by archaeologists precisely because of the traces of fire. The same thing, in some way, had happened to Teotihuacán. Fire, which served for praying, ended up destroying the cities: a lesson about the two faces of what is revered.

So, when you look at the brazier, do not think only of the smoke. Think of continuity: a thread that runs from the figurine of Cuicuilco, passes through Teotihuacán, reaches Tula, and continues in the copal burners of today.

texto.Material: Hand-molded clay painted in several colors with mineral pigments

texto.pregunta: Myth: Copal only served to give off a pleasant scent.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It was an offering: its smoke was considered food and message for the gods.
